summary: The bill bans social media accounts for children under 13, prohibits personalized recommendation algorithms for users under 17, and requires schools receiving federal internet subsidies to block student access to social media platforms on school devices and networks.

scores.thoughts: The bill creates new regulatory requirements enforced by the FTC and FCC but contains no appropriations, new programs requiring funding, or spending reductions. Any enforcement costs would be marginal and incidental.
The bill contains no tax provisions, credits, deductions, or revenue measures of any kind.
No provisions relate to healthcare delivery, insurance, public coverage, or market-based reforms.
No provisions address firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration, border policy, visas, or protections for non-citizens.
No provisions address reproductive rights, abortion access, or related regulations.
No provisions address military, defense, or national security spending or policy.
No provisions address environmental regulations, climate policy, or energy.
No provisions address welfare programs, food assistance, or other safety-net benefits.

Title II amends the Children’s Internet Protection Act to condition school broadband subsidies on blocking social media access and adopting specific internet safety policies. This increases federal regulatory involvement in school technology use and policy, which aligns with the negative end of the scale (greater federal involvement in public education).
No provisions address drug enforcement, decriminalization, or controlled substances.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, rehabilitation, or criminal procedure.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization.
No provisions address deficits, debt reduction, or fiscal policy.
No provisions address legal protections or restrictions related to LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance or international aid.
No provisions address voting access, election integrity, or electoral procedures.

The bill imposes new restrictions on social media platforms’ use of personalized recommendation systems for users under 17, requires deletion of children’s personal data, limits data retention for compliance, and mandates blocking/filtering on school networks. These are clear expansions of regulatory oversight and data-protection requirements on technology companies.
No provisions address worker protections, union rights, or employer flexibility.
No provisions address religious exemptions or civil-rights enforcement.
